item.title: India’s Student Protesters Win Some Concessions From Government
item.description:
The student protests that have gripped India sent thousands of young people into the streets on Friday, where some were beaten by the police, as the government sought to buy time in negotiations with the movement’s leaders without conceding to their central demand.

In Mumbai and New Delhi, thousands of demonstrators turned out again to vent their anger over a botched medical school entrance examination that affected millions of young people, and a wider sense of frustration about a lack of jobs and opportunity. In Kolkata, police used batons to disperse crowds of thousands, according to local media reports, and there were demonstrations in Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune and Jaipur, as protests reached cities across India on Friday.

The youth-led protest movement is posing one of the most substantial challenges in years to the leadership of India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi. Many of the protesters are students, and others are working, but they share a sense of desperation and rage about education and employment prospects. Their anger is hard for Mr. Modi to ignore, with young people accounting for 40 percent of India’s population.

The self-described Cockroach Janta Party, which derived its name from an insult, is the driving force behind the protests. The group said on Friday that it would press for demonstrations nationally until Dharmendra Pradhan, India’s education minister, stepped down, a demand it has framed as nonnegotiable.

The group holds Mr. Pradhan directly accountable for the leak of the exams, which led to canceled results. But he is a key operative in Mr. Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, credited with helping the party come to power in some recent state elections.

After talks with government ministers on Friday, Ashutosh Ranka, a spokesman for the protesters, said in a social media statement that the government had agreed “in principle” to compensate families affected by the suicides of students and would take “no legal action against protesters.” According to the C.J.P., at least 21 students have died by suicide since the exam leak, unable to handle the stress.

The government has requested more time to respond to the demand for the removal of the education minister, and another round of discussions is planned for Saturday.

Saurav Das, another spokesman for the protesters, said that, once they had achieved their main goal, the resignation of Mr. Pradhan, the group would also ask the government to consider its far more sweeping agenda for change, including judicial reforms, gender quotas for Parliament and punishments for politicians who switch political parties after being elected.

The prospect of an organized, student-led opposition to Mr. Modi, an acutely image-conscious leader, has added a new challenge to his recent days in office. He is also managing economic difficulties caused by the war in Iran and recently led his party to power in a series of state elections.

Some of the students’ fury is turning directly on him, but his response so far does not appear to have satisfied them. On Thursday, he posted on social media that “Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth!” He has promised fast-track tribunals to punish those responsible for the exam leak. Even that acknowledgment was rare for Mr. Modi, a strongman leader, who must balance the need to placate the students with a desire to make sure that his political party does not look weak.

The protests in New Delhi and elsewhere have been going on for more than a month. But the protesters’ call to march to Parliament on July 20, its first day in session, has given the movement momentum. Thousands of people gathered in the capital for the march, and many have remained camped out at the protest site for days despite the authorities’ calls to disperse.

Anupreeta Das, Alex Travelli and Mujib Mashal contributed reporting.

item.title: Chief Prosecutor of International Court Is Removed After Sexual Misconduct Charge
item.description:
Karim A. A. Khan, the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, has been removed from his position, the court’s oversight body announced on Friday, after a 20-month-long investigation into allegations that he sexually harassed a subordinate.

The decision came down to an assessment that Mr. Khan had committed “serious misconduct” and a breach of duty.

The I.C.C.’s Assembly of States Parties, the governing body that brings together its 125 member nations, made the decision during a session in New York on Friday. A substantial majority of its members, 82, voted to remove Mr. Khan, according to an official statement released Friday afternoon in New York.

The decision is one that victims’ rights groups and outside watchdogs have been pushing for, but will leave the criminal court searching for leadership at a difficult moment. The investigation into Mr. Khan left the institution without its most visible face for much of the past two years, damaging its credibility at the same time it has confronted attacks from the Trump administration.

Mr. Khan rocketed to global prominence after he issued an arrest warrant for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in 2023, and warrants for Hamas officials and Israeli leaders, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in 2024.

The United States, which is among the countries that have not signed onto the I.C.C., has objected to Mr. Khan’s charges against Israeli officials, and the Trump administration earlier this month announced plans to “dismantle” the court.

The removal of Mr. Khan could leave the court in limbo at a moment when it is working on several high-profile cases. Arrest warrants for Israeli leaders remain active; a case against the former president of the Philippines, Rodrigo Duterte, has been proceeding; a Libyan militia commander was arrested earlier this year, and an application for an arrest warrant related to crimes against the Rohingya population in Myanmar has been under review.

Mr. Khan has consistently denied the allegations against him, and his lawyers said in a statement on Friday that “the decision is unsupported by any lawful or properly reasoned finding.”

Mr. Khan’s lawyers pointed to “serious defects” in the process, arguing that the investigation did not prove that sexual misconduct had occurred and that Mr. Khan was not given a comprehensive chance to respond.

“Mr. Khan will challenge the lawfulness and fairness of the decision through all available legal mechanisms,” they said.

Even so, some external legal experts greeted the decision as a chance for the court to move on at a time when its very existence is under threat.

“The world in general has moved away from international institutions and solutions,” said Alex Whiting, a professor at Harvard Law School, who said that he thought that the process was ultimately fair, if messy, and that the chance to appoint a new chief prosecutor would give the institution a fresh start.

“I think the court will be able to move past this,” Mr. Whiting said.

But closure may be difficult. A new chief prosecutor will need to be elected. And just on Friday, Venezuela, its government newly under Trump administration direction, announced that it was withdrawing from the I.C.C.

“Damage has been done, and it will take a long time to repair and recover,” said Ezequiel Jimenez Martinez, the author of a recent book on International Criminal Court governance.

Accusations against Mr. Khan first surfaced internally in early 2024. Sarah, a lawyer from Malaysia who was then working as a special assistant to Mr. Khan, suggested to colleagues that she was being pressured to engage in sexual activities with Mr. Khan against her will, and they reported the situation internally.

Sarah declined to file a formal complaint so no formal investigation was started then. (Sarah has recently made her story public, speaking to news outlets on condition of using only her first name.)

But by that autumn, newspapers had begun to report on the existence of the complaint and its fallout.

After the allegations became public, the I.C.C.’s governing body announced an independent investigation.

A team from the United Nations was asked to look into the allegations. A panel of judges then reviewed the team’s findings. Mr. Khan went on voluntary leave from his position after the investigation began and was later suspended as it proceeded.

While the U.N. investigators said they found evidence that Mr. Khan engaged in “non-consensual sexual contact” with Sarah, the judges determined unanimously that it did not meet the “beyond a reasonable doubt” legal standard for a finding of misconduct.

Despite that, the I.C.C.’s executive body later concluded that Mr. Khan had sexually harassed Sarah, finding “beyond a reasonable doubt” that the prosecutor had engaged in a sexual relationship with her, and that “in the context of that power imbalance a sexual relationship could never be appropriate.”

In her talks with investigators through the years and in an interview last week with CNN, Sarah described how sexual attention from Mr. Khan escalated over time, starting after she began working for him as an assistant in 2023.

She said Mr. Khan used their proximity on work trips to pursue a sexual relationship with her.

The international court, officially established in 2002 and based in The Hague, has a mission to investigate and prosecute genocide, war crimes and other serious offenses.

Mr. Khan was elected by the I.C.C.’s participating countries in 2021 to serve a nine-year term, and the investigation into his conduct has left the court in a state of extended uncertainty. Some of his supporters have suggested that the case was an attempt to undermine him and the court, perhaps in response to his actions against Israel.

Josep Borrell, the former top diplomat at the European Union, wrote in a post on Project Syndicate last week that the situation was “sabotage dressed up in the language of good-faith inquiry and accountability.”

Mr. Borrell wrote that “the Trump administration and Netanyahu want the same thing: to ensure that no international court can touch soldiers, border agents, or its chosen allies, no matter how serious the allegations of war crimes and crimes against humanity.”

In a July interview with The New York Times, Sarah said that she was frustrated with claims that her allegations were in some way related to Mr. Khan’s decisions to seek warrants against high-profile leaders.

“Victims do not choose the political calendar of their abusers,” she said. “There is never a right time.”

One question now is whether the outcome will enable the court’s opponents to undermine it.

“The long-delayed removal of Karim Khan from the ICC for serious misconduct has exposed the moral bankruptcy of a corrupt Prosecutor,” Gideon Saar, the Israeli foreign minister, wrote on social media.

He argued that the warrants against Mr. Netanyahu and other Israeli leaders were filed to deflect from Mr. Khan’s sexual harassment complaints, and “should be revoked immediately.”

item.title: A Once Outlawed Māori Art Form Is Alive and in the Flesh
item.description:
Mark Kopua pressed his face close as he drew on his nephew’s arm with a felt-tip marker. From memory, he sketched patterns and motifs that had been in their family for generations. Finally satisfied, he pulled on rubber gloves and a needle gun buzzed to life.

This was no regular tattoo. This was tā moko, the ritual body art practiced for centuries by the Māori, the Indigenous inhabitants of New Zealand. Half a dozen of Mr. Kopua’s relatives observed the ritual in February, squeezing into his small studio in Gisborne, on the east coast of New Zealand’s North Island.

Mr. Kopua, 64, and his nephew, Desmond Horomia, 56, grew up in a Māori community that had lost all its tohunga tā moko, or ritual tattoo artists. The craft had been traditionally handed down from parent to child, but in 1907, New Zealand’s British colonial rulers banned tā moko and other Indigenous art forms. Māori people began hiding their tattoos and stopped teaching younger generations.

More than a century later, the facial tattoos known as moko kanohi are being seen again, on television, on the streets and in the halls of New Zealand’s Parliament. Maori teens and young adults have taken to documenting their tā moko ceremonies on social media. Some have convinced their elders to be tattooed, helping the art form make a jubilant comeback after decades of stigma.

“I’ve been involved with this for well over 30 years now, but our culture is still relearning because they’ve been immersed and overwhelmed by Western culture,” Mr. Kopua said.

Mr. Kopua and a small group of other artisans began tattooing faces after a Māori nationalist movement gained ground in the 1970s.

“Moko was asleep at the time. We decided we want to wake this thing back up again,” he said.

A moko kanohi is the work of a lifetime. A person’s history can be gleaned from the tattoos on their face, signifying their ancestry and marking their coming of age, the birth of a child or the death of a relative.

Women are marked on their lips and chin with moko kauae. Men receive mataora, which starts on the chin and grows outward to mark personal milestones. Family trees can be traced through recurring patterns on different faces.

“It’s a thumbprint of your genealogy,” said Ruihana Smith, 32, a woodcarver who is an adviser on Māori relations to the Marlborough District Council in the South Island town of Blenheim.

He received a mataora in 2023 to honor his great-grandmother after her death. It took four and a half hours to tattoo Mr. Smith’s chin, nose and cheeks as family members watched.

In some tā moko ceremonies, relatives sing blessings and hold the person’s hands and arms as they undergo the ritual. While today’s tā moko artists use modern tattoo machines, traditionally the tohunga would use blades carved from shark teeth or the wing bones of an albatross, Mr. Kopua said.

Without forebears to teach them, Mr. Kopua — a tohunga whakairo, or a master woodcarver — learned tā moko from the patterns he used in carving and weaving. They studied moko kanohi patterns on decapitated heads that were under the care of New Zealand’s national museum.

Māori warriors believed that decapitation severed their enemies’ connection to the gods. In the 19th century, British settlers collected the heads as curiosities and trophies and offered guns and gold in exchange — prompting some Māori people to hunt down those who wore mataora and moko kauae.

“That was one thing that stopped our ancestors from wanting to get their faces tattooed,” Mr. Kopua said.

Māori who converted to Christianity at the time were also discouraged from getting tattoos. The ultimate blow, however, came with the Tohunga Suppression Act in 1907, which outlawed Māori experts, including priests, healers, teachers, woodcarvers and tattoo artists. The legislation, aimed at prohibiting practices that the authorities deemed exploitative, suffocated Māori culture for decades.

New Zealand’s Parliament repealed the law in 1962. But for years afterward, moko kanohi was seen as the sign of a criminal or a gang member, Mr. Smith said.

“None of the art forms are illegal any more, but we have to undo the damage,” he said.

Tame Iti, one of the leaders of the 1970s Māori protest movement, has moko that spiral across his face, from his forehead, past his neck and over his ears. The 74-year-old recalls growing up at a time when hotels and other public venues barred anyone with facial markings. He ran for Parliament four times, none of them successful, but became a national figure.

Mr. Iti’s last attempt to enter Parliament was in 2014. Two years later, Nanaia Mahuta became the first woman to wear moko kauae in the House of Representatives, the sole chamber of New Zealand’s Parliament. She served as foreign minister under Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern.

“Now you’ve got politicians, judges, all kinds of people with moko. It’s beautiful that it’s out there,” Mr. Iti said.

Young Māori have been quicker to embrace tā moko than their elders, said Ed Harawira, 50, a tā moko artist. A New Zealand government survey in 2018, the most recently available, found that more than a quarter of Māori people ages 25 to 44 had traditional tattoos, the most of any age group, compared with 8 percent of those 55 and older.

“Our older people were the ones who initially opposed receiving moko because they had been oppressed for so many years,” Mr. Harawira said, adding: “They were brought up thinking that Māori culture wasn’t going to get us anywhere in today’s civilization.”

After the birth of her fourth child, Huirangi Law, 36, decided to become the first person in her family in three generations to receive moko. Though she considered how the outside world might perceive her differently, “I knew wholeheartedly in my soul that this is who I was, and this is what I wanted to do,” she said. “The spaces, jobs, careers, anything like that — they would come naturally.”

Children can start receiving moko kanohi from age 13, Mr. Smith said. Younger children, like his 9-year-old daughter and 5-year-old son, wear temporary tattoos to copy their parents. Mr. Smith said he started to learn tā moko with the goal of giving his children tattoos someday.

Mr. Kopua said he has been training students to pass tā moko down to future generations.

“That’s how we maintain it,” he said. “Not just to wake the art up, but to keep it awake.”

item.title: As Trump Escalates Trade War, Some Canadian Premiers Want to Hit Back
item.description:
This week President Trump signed an order imposing 50 percent tariffs on a wide array of Canadian exports in retaliation for Canada’s retaliation on his earlier tariffs, and some Canadian premiers were soon urging even more revenge.

[Read: Trump to Impose 50% Tariff on Many Canadian Goods]

[Read: Trump Is Squeezing Canada. Don’t Expect Carney to Roll Over.]

Doug Ford, Ontario’s premier, called on Ottawa to block or limit exports of potash, important minerals and energy, including oil and electricity. All of those items, which are among Canada’s largest exports, are excluded from the new tariffs taking effect on Aug. 19.

“They need to feel the pain,” Mr. Ford said.

The tariffs dominated talk at the premiers’ annual summer meeting this week in Charlottetown. Susan Holt, the premier of New Brunswick, home to a large oil refinery that provides the Boston area with much of its gasoline, also raised the possibility of striking back with energy restrictions.

“We put gas in their cars, we put jet fuel in their fighter jets, and we heat and cool their homes,” Mr. Holt said. “So we know that we have those kinds of tools at our disposal.”

And business leaders and other politicians across the country are pushing for more tariffs on imports from the United States, like the 25 percent one Canada put on cars after Mr. Trump imposed one on Canadian-made cars.

After meeting with the premiers, Prime Minister Mark Carney wouldn’t exclude retaliation from the government’s list of possible responses.

(I’ve written a guide to the latest round of tariffs: What to Know About Trump’s Tariffs on Canada, and What’s Next.)

[Read: New Tariffs as Old Ones Expire: The Latest on Trump’s Trade War]

While more retaliation may be popular among many Canadians, it’s not an idea widely endorsed by economists.

“I understand the frustration,” said Daniel Trefler, an economic analyst with the Rotman School of Business at the University of Toronto. “But the first important thing about retaliation is that for every dollar of harm to the U.S. — by harm I mean lower wages, lower G.D.P. — we take about $4 of harm when we retaliate.”

The harm to Canada, he said, comes mainly in the form of higher prices. Small manufacturers, for example, generally cannot shift even most of their steel purchases to Canadian mills because the steel makers are oriented toward large buyers like automakers. The result is that the tariff-inflated prices manufacturers pay for steel imported from the United States are compounded several times before products finally reach consumers.

But Professor Telfer said that retaliation by Canada is also undermined by several political realities.

“Our economy is much more exposed to the U.S. than the U.S. economy is exposed to us,” he said. “So it’s much easier for them to hurt us than for us to hurt them.”

He agrees that restricting the supply of energy and potash or greatly boosting their prices to American buyers could be an effective weapon, but he quickly added: “Politically, it’s a nonstarter.”

At the premiers’ meeting, both Danielle Smith, the premier of oil-rich Alberta, and Scott Moe, her counterpart in Saskatchewan, which is laden with potash, flatly rejected the idea.

“You’re asking them to bear the brunt of this policy, I just don’t see it working,” he told me.

Worse, he said, the use of those resources or electricity from Quebec as a pressure tactic would likely feed separatist sentiments in both regions.

So what should Mr. Carney do? Professor Telfer recommends patience.

The regulation of international trade constitutionally falls to Congress, not the president, in the United States. Mr. Trump has taken trade powers Congress has granted to presidents far beyond how they were intended to be used.

If, as may be likely, the Democrats take back control of the House of Representatives in the midterm elections in November, Professor Telfer anticipates that Congress will move quickly to rein in Mr. Trump on trade.

“So let’s play the waiting game,” he said. “So just stay calm, everybody, and think what’s in Canada’s best interest, and take anger out of the equation.”

Ian Austen reports on Canada for The Times. A Windsor, Ontario, native now based in Ottawa, he has reported on the country for two decades. He can be reached at austen@nytimes.com.

By Vjosa Isai

Wildfires have razed millions of forest acres in northwestern Ontario this month, uprooted remote communities and polluted the air as far away as Washington.

Late last week, the photographer Cole Burston and I flew two hours north of Toronto, where we are based, to Thunder Bay, Ontario, the city nearest the fires, to report on the evacuations and firefighting effort.

We drove hundreds of miles around the region that is especially popular with wilderness outfitters from the United States for pristine lakes, backcountry canoeing and endless boreal forest. Canada’s natural beauty is breathtaking in the north — not just the sights, but the smells. Four days after we arrived, the acrid wildfire smoke had cleared significantly and a fragrant, tea-like aroma wafted from the pine trees around the fire hall in a rural community called Nolalu.

The scent lured me out of the open garage door and I waved over Val Warner, the first response coordinator on the fire team comprised entirely of volunteers, to ask, “What is that smell?”

“Fresh air,” Ms. Warner responded, not missing a beat and clearly amused, as was I, with her jab at city folk. (In true Canadian fashion, she immediately apologized, though she had nothing to be sorry about.)

Her lighthearted joke played into a running theme of our reporting in the north: the rural-urban divide. Those fissures deepened during the wildfire evacuations as residents blamed politicians in Toronto for ignoring the needs of northerners, and for endangering them by providing spotty communication about the fires. Some evacuees described feeling left to fend for themselves, and a group of First Nations leaders are now calling for a public inquiry into the government’s response.

[Read: ‘Help Never Came.’ Canadian Wildfire Evacuees Want to Know Why.]

Evacuees recounted the harrowing details of their escape. In Namaygoosisagagun First Nation, about 155 miles north of Thunder Bay but inaccessible by car, residents leaped into small fishing boats and fled across the lake as a fire came, seemingly out of nowhere, to their doorstep.

[Read: Evacuees of Ontario’s Wildfires Wait and Worry]

Many of the people I spoke to demanded accountability, which is an important function of journalism and why institutions like The New York Times send reporters to disaster scenes. But a challenge of covering wildfires in Canada is the lack of access to the front lines. Ontario’s Ministry of Natural Resources, the provincial department responsible for forest management, denied our request to photograph the wildfire response. The ministry also would not allow us to visit the fire crews staging at camps located a major distance from the blazes.

Ontario’s position is not an outlier. Photographers have largely been barred from documenting the work of firefighters across the country, including by the governments of British Columbia and Alberta. The Globe and Mail, Canada’s national newspaper, put it aptly in a 2024 column by its editorial board: “Where there’s smoke, there’s a smoke screen.”

The policy to broadly deny these requests from journalists, barring safety risks, is different from some jurisdictions in the United States like California where the law protects such access for journalists.

Around Thunder Bay, road blockades warned of fines and tickets by the police. Some residents we spoke to defied the orders, but didn’t want to run the risk of having reporters in their vehicles.

After closely studying maps and driving for hours along bumpy dirt paths, Cole and I managed to document some of the aftermath in areas where road access was not restricted, and where the fire had long been gone.

Eventually, our luck ran out. A conservation officer approached Cole when he was parked to file his pictures. Though the main highway wasn’t blocked, the officer still warned him to leave.

President Trump threatened to impose tariffs on Canada because the smoke spewed across many cities in the United States. On a visit to Thunder Bay, Premier Ford responded that Americans should be supporting Canada during a wildfire crisis, not punishing the country.

The smoke set poor air quality records for many towns and cities in Canada and the United States, an analysis shows. And for firefighters, enduring high temperatures make it even more difficult to control and extinguish blazes.

My colleague Norimitsu Onishi explained why many of Canada’s wildfires are impossible to put out.

Dave Wallace-Wells, an Opinion writer at The Times, argues that society must adapt to smoky seasons as “nothing can prevent the new wildfires.”

Vjosa Isai is a Toronto-based reporter for The Times covering Canada.

Norimitsu, our Montreal correspondent, and the photographer Renaud Philippe, traveled to Nunavut and reported on Jacinto Marques, who left Angola for Canada’s Arctic. Now he’s running a bus service in Iqaluit, and a road to nowhere has a new stop.

Ian Austen reported on the Gordie Howe International Bridge, which finally opened on Friday after a delay ordered by President Trump and new tariffs against Canada. But Americans were disinvited from the ceremony.

Jacob Tsimerman, a professor of mathematics at the University of Toronto, won one of four Fields Medals, an award for top mathematicians under 40, for his work on the André-Oort conjecture.

For over a decade, something strange has been happening in a lake straddling the border of Quebec and Vermont. Lake Memphremagog is home to brown bullhead catfish, and anglers began noticing that some were covered in velvety black growths.

A large investment firm and a Canadian uranium mining and enrichment company made a big bet three years ago on nuclear power. Now, that wager is proving prescient.

World Cup winners and losers off the field: Host cities, hotels, tourism boards and more had lofty expectations for the 39-day tournament. Some struck gold but others fizzled. See how Toronto and Vancouver fared.

From Opinion: Iran, China, Canada? A defense of Trump’s grand strategy.

How are we doing?We’re eager to have your thoughts about this newsletter and events in Canada in general. Please send them to nytcanada@nytimes.com.

item.title: Canadian Intern at NATO Military HQ Is Arrested on Suspicion of Spying
item.description:
The authorities in Belgium said on Saturday that a Canadian intern at the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s military headquarters had been arrested on suspicion of spying for another country.

The Belgian Federal Prosecutor’s Office said the woman was “of Chinese origin” and was arrested on Friday. “She is suspected of spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization,” it said in a statement, which did not identify the country or the criminal organization.

The intern was first flagged by the security services at the Supreme Headquarters Allied Command Europe, or SHAPE, which is near Mons, Belgium. The case was then referred to Belgian intelligence and a police investigation was launched, the federal prosecutor’s office said.

That investigation led to searches of the woman’s home and place of work on Thursday, and a judge decided to place her under arrest on Friday, the prosecutor’s office said, adding in its statement that it would not comment further on the case.

Canada’s Foreign Ministry and the Canadian Embassy in Brussels did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Saturday.

SHAPE, which plans and executes NATO’s military operations, was cooperating with the Belgian authorities, said Col. Martin O’Donnell, a SHAPE spokesman.

“At this time, there is no indication that NATO or SHAPE operational readiness, command and control arrangements, or ongoing tasks have been adversely affected,” he said in a statement.

Lara Jakes contributed reporting.

item.title: Taiwan Tests How It Would Resist a Chinese Siege at Sea
item.description:
As armed Chinese ships expand patrols around Taiwan, officials in Taipei are more urgently testing how they would keep fuel and other vital supplies flowing if Beijing tried to choke off the island.

China, which claims Taiwan as its territory, has in recent years rehearsed a blockade, using naval ships and military planes to practice sealing off access to Taiwan.

Taiwan relies on imports of fossil fuels for about 95 percent of its energy, and natural gas fuels half of its power generation. And the global shocks caused by the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz during the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran have highlighted the importance of securing energy supplies.

Officials in Taiwan are exploring whether floating gas storage and processing terminals, emergency stockpiles, or even reviving nuclear power could help keep the island running in a crisis.

They have held so-called tabletop, or wargaming, exercises to address a siege scenario, and are planning to conduct drills to escort and reroute ships to port and to store and distribute supplies on Taiwan, four officials said. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal government deliberations.

Worries about the threats posed by China have sharpened since last month, when Beijing announced its coast guard ships would conduct “routine law-enforcement patrols” in the waters east of Taiwan. That expanse of ocean matters because it is where Taiwan would most likely look for the United States and its allies to bring military and economic relief if China attacked.

Keeping power plants supplied during a Chinese blockade would be daunting. Taiwan maintains at least 11 days’ worth of natural gas reserves, and has the capacity to store enough for up to 20 days.

“We’ve constantly conducted exercises on these national security topics, figuring out how to handle different scenarios,” Chen Chung-hsien, a deputy director-general of Taiwan’s Energy Administration, said in an interview. “We certainly view matters using worst-case scenarios.”

Taiwan is exploring acquiring ships for storing and processing natural gas off shore, to provide additional capacity and for emergencies, Mr. Chen said.

Chen Kuan-ting, a lawmaker from Taiwan’s governing Democratic Progressive Party who focuses on national security issues, said such ships could give Taiwan “more flexibility for how natural gas is received and dispatched” if China tries to seal off the island and threaten its infrastructure.

But finding safer gas reception sites remains a big challenge.

Taiwan’s three terminals for receiving and storing liquefied natural gas are on the island’s west, where they would be highly exposed to attack or harassment from China during a crisis. The east coast is forbiddingly mountainous, with relatively narrow roads and small ports with no infrastructure for taking delivery from hulking natural gas tankers, or generating and distributing power from the gas.

“The eastern region wouldn’t necessarily be the best solution,” said Mr. Chen, the energy official. “A floating pier on the west coast is more plausible, closer to existing power plants anyway.”

Taiwan’s government is also weighing whether to reverse its closure of nuclear power plants, which could be one source of stable power.

Craig Singleton, the China program senior director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies in Washington, said his group held a tabletop exercise about a Chinese “energy siege” of Taiwan last year with senior Taiwanese officials and company leaders. It was clear that “Taiwan urgently needed to diversify both its energy suppliers and the means by which those supplies reach the island before a crisis,” he said.

Even as they grapple with the threat of invasion, Taiwan’s officials are preparing for a murkier kind of coercion, in which Chinese government ships warn, restrict or even board cargo vessels approaching Taiwan.

The ships China has positioned on Taiwan’s east coast are part of what officials call “gray zone” tactics — hardball actions that fall short of outright warfare. Such muscle-flexing is hard for Taiwan to counter without risking retaliation from China.

Beijing has declared its jurisdiction over the waters in that area, a claim Taiwan rejects. In an early sign of how China could use its presence to assert its claims, a Chinese government ship stationed east of Taiwan radioed three passing cargo ships to request information, including about the crew members onboard.

“What they did east of Taiwan was partly a very initial exercise to model a quarantine, meaning an operation to inspect and possibly turn back ships at sea,” said Lai I-chung, the president of the Prospect Foundation, a foreign policy institute in Taipei.

China’s navy regularly places about seven or eight naval ships around Taiwan, including off the island’s east coast, according to Taiwanese security officials.

“But now we’re also seeing more and more of the China Coast Guard,” Mr. Lai said, noting he was speaking in a personal capacity. The increased presence of the coast guard — a paramilitary force with large, heavily armed ships — would increase Beijing’s choices to put pressure on Taiwan.

During a tabletop simulation late last month, President Lai Ching-te of Taiwan and his senior officials worked through a scenario in which Beijing demanded that cargo ships seek its approval before approaching Taiwan and sent coast guard ships to board, inspect and seize vessels. (In 2024, a Chinese coast guard patrol briefly boarded a Taiwanese ferry.)

Lii Wen, a Taiwanese national security official who described the exercise in a speech afterward, said that it “helped to pinpoint shortcomings in current response measures” and heightened attention on improving coordination between agencies on issues such as ensuring energy supplies. He declined a request for an interview.

The Ministry of the Interior, which helped organize the June simulation, announced this year that it was planning disaster response drills on the east coast of Taiwan in September that would test receiving international medical teams and supplies.

Other exercises will most likely train officials from the ministries for the interior, economic affairs and agriculture to work together on distributing supplies within Taiwan. Escorting of ships approaching Taiwan would fall under its Navy and Coast Guard.

The Chinese coast guard ships currently off Taiwan’s east seem to be serving a mostly symbolic role for now. But that could change, Ryan D. Martinson, an associate professor at the U.S. Naval War College, said in emailed comments, also speaking in his personal capacity.

“Once the ships are out there on a consistent basis, Beijing is in a better position to take more forceful actions against Taiwan,” he wrote.

The two coast guard ships China sent to Taiwan’s east this month weigh 3,000 and 4,000 metric tons, far larger than the coast guard boats Taiwan sent to shadow them. Ships from the Chinese Maritime Safety Administration, which regulates civilian shipping, also took part in recent actions in the same area.

Chinese government ships sailed near Taiwan’s main island 85 times during May and June, compared with 45 times in the same period last year, the Taiwan Coast Guard has estimated.

Coast guard ships come under Chinese military command and have been increasingly integrated in military exercises near Taiwan, said Julia Famularo, a lecturer at the University of Hawaii at Manoa who studies China’s maritime operations.

The pressure from Beijing could increase before and after 2028, when Taiwan holds its next presidential election, said Taiwanese officials and experts.

“I think these gray zone measures will definitely become more and more intense,” said Jing Yuan-chou, an adjunct professor at Tamkang University in Taiwan, who studies China’s military strategy toward Taiwan.

“For now, they prefer nibbling away at us, piece by piece,” Mr. Jing said. “But the nibbling lays the way for if they ever want to try to devour us.”

item.title: Wildfire Smoke Chokes Skies in Spain and France
item.description:
Wildfires in France and Spain this past week have blazed toward cities, forced evacuations by land and sea and wreathed the skies of southern Europe in stifling smoke.

Already broiling under intense summer heat, some 200,000 people in France and Spain have fled their homes or were ordered to remain indoors as dozens of fires moved across parts of each country. In France, one official called two severe fires the “ogres of the summer.” In Spain, another labeled one blaze “the worst wildfire in the Madrid region’s history.”

The Spanish government has declared the fires in the Madrid region a national emergency, and both countries have requested additional aid from the European Union to combat the fires and help people affected.

Firefighters battled flames on Friday in a forest in Lège-Cap-Ferret, in southwestern France.

A French Civil Security aircraft flying past flames on Thursday in a forest surrounding Cotignac, in southeastern France.

Students from a martial arts gym worked to extinguish a fire outside their teacher’s home on Friday in the village of El Tiemblo, Spain.

People who left Lège-Cap-Ferret arrived in Arcachon, across the Arcachon Bay, during an evacuation of the Cap Ferret peninsula in France on Friday.

Evacuees sheltered from wildfires on Friday in Cebreros, Spain, west of Madrid.

Traffic jams built up from the areas threatened by the fire. Cap Ferret, a popular vacation destination, is a geographically isolated peninsula with one major road going in and out.

Smoke darkened the skies near the beach on Thursday in Andernos-les-Bains, in southwestern France.

Juana Gonzalez, a resident of El Tiemblo, Spain, covered her face to protect herself from smoke on Friday.

Firefighters in Spain carried out controlled burns in the village of Navas del Rey to slow the spread of wildfires.

A firefighter working near a burning building on Thursday in Lège-Cap-Ferret, France.

Some evacuees in Spain took shelter from the wildfires in a Madrid sports center.

A wildfire burned in a forest near the Arcachon Bay on Friday.

item.title: Who Are the People Protesting in India?
item.description:
The pent-up hopes and frustrations of India’s young people found a release in a protest movement that gathered steam this past week in the capital, New Delhi.

A crowd of thousands was mobilized by a call by the leaders of a youth movement to reform India’s troubled education system and to push for the resignation of the country’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, whom they blamed for a botched college-entrance exam that left millions in the lurch.

On Saturday, Mr. Pradhan submitted his resignation to Mr. Modi, handing the protesters a major win. But it wasn’t immediately clear that the protesters would call it a day given that their grievances have grown since a violent crackdown by police on Monday. The beating of demonstrators fueled people’s anger and the spirit of the protests has become more inclusive, attracting activists and academics, curious teenagers, blue-collar parents and children from affluent homes, established celebrities and newly minted influencers, atheists, farmers, religious leaders, and even a man wearing a Spiderman mask.

The movement may continue to pose one of the most substantial challenges in years to the leadership of India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi. The anger is hard for him to ignore, with young people accounting for 40 percent of India’s population.

Here are some of their voices:

AMAL HAYAT, 20

Amal Hayat, 20, a student of electrical and computer engineering at Delhi’s Jamia Millia Islamia University, is the kind of young person whose ambitions are essential to Mr. Modi’s vision of a “Vikshit Bharat,” or developed India, by 2047.

She is the first woman in her family to go to college — a point of pride — and said she chose engineering because she had a head for math and wanted to pursue a career in artificial intelligence. “Solving problems gives me peace,” she said.

She joined the protests not because of a person, or a political party or movement. “It’s about the issues, the students, it’s about the future of the country,” she said.

And, for her, it’s about fairness. She walked around the protest grounds on Thursday afternoon, holding a large sheet of paper on which she had scrawled in black ink: “Sticks for students, garlands for rapists.”

Ms. Hayat, 20, said she was making a point about impunity. She contrasted the batons used by security forces to hit protesters as they marched toward Parliament on Monday, to the treatment of some Indian politicians who continue to enjoy the perks of public life even as they face criminal cases against them for serious charges, including rape.

“So what kind of justice is this?” she asked.

ANSHU GUDIYA, 13

Anshu Gudiya, an eighth-grader who lives in Faridabad, a city in the greater Delhi area, said she came to the protests to see what the fuss was all about, even if it meant taking a day off from school.

Her father works in a hotel in Delhi, and her mother is a tailor. Her parents allowed her to go by herself, she said, because the scandal that ignited the protest movement — the botched college exam — “also affects my future.”

Science is her favorite subject at school, Anshu said, and she wants to study machine learning and artificial intelligence, two subjects that require government-administered exams to get into top public engineering schools. She has not thought about her future beyond that, but hopes someday to “work at Google.”

Anshu said it took her more than three hours, after multiple train changes and a ride on a rented bike, to reach the protest site, next to the 18th-century Jantar Mantar observatory. She came prepared for Delhi’s merciless sun, with a head scarf and sunscreen.

She had first heard about the protests and the group behind them, the Cockroach Janta Party, on Instagram. “I also wanted to see the protest for myself,” and to understand how people conduct demonstrations against the government, said Anshu.

CHANDAN KUMAR, 28

Chandan Kumar, 28, is a delivery driver, not a student, but the protest movement’s demands resonated with him.

Like millions of India’s young people, he was forced to choose between pursuing school and finding a job. He said he dropped out of high school after his mother fell ill, and the family needed extra income to cover her medical costs. He found work in construction, and eventually gave up his dreams of going back to school.

At one point, he said he learned how to use Excel and interviewed for data entry jobs, but could not type fast enough. In 2018, he found a job as a delivery agent for a popular online food platform. “When a person is left with no options, they have to do whatever comes their way,” Mr. Kumar said.

The work is “decent enough,” Mr. Kumar said, as he sat on his motorbike, taking a break from delivering food that customers had ordered for the protesters, from pizza to vegetable curry.

Mr. Kumar said he supported the protesters’ demand that the education minister resign. He was hopeful that the education system would be fixed so that his child can have a better future. “Compared to where I am, my child will reach a place that is a hundred times better.”

ZAFAR HABIB

Zafar Habib’s future doesn’t directly rest on the outcome of the protest movement. The son of a math professor and an activist mother, Mr. Habib, 22, is a history graduate from a private university, and is headed to Oxford University for further studies.

But although he said he had not faced the same educational challenges, he joined the protests out of solidarity and a sense that the outpouring of anger is a significant moment for the country.

People who had grown up seeing little other than “bigotry, fear-mongering and hatred” under Mr. Modi’s Hindu nationalist government, which has been in power since 2014, were getting the chance to “express a love for each other,” he said. It resonated with him as a Muslim, Mr. Habib said, adding that he had suffered taunts as a child because of his last name.

People were helping each other, handing out free food and water, and joining hands to be heard, he said. The humanity he has witnessed made Mr. Habib hopeful that once people go back to their daily lives, “we will carry this kindness forward.”

item.title: What to Know About the Wildfires Raging in Western Europe
item.description:
Fast-moving wildfires fueled by extreme heat and strong winds have forced some 200,000 people to flee or remain indoors this past week in France and Spain as firefighters struggle to bring the blazes under control.

No deaths have been linked to the fires, which have mainly hit southwestern France, near Bordeaux, and central Spain, near Madrid.

But the flames have torn through tens of thousands of acres of land, injured dozens of firefighters, destroyed scores of homes and campsites and forced many vacationers to flee popular summertime spots.

The Spanish and French authorities have requested additional resources from the European Union and warned that high temperatures and erratic gusts were making it difficult to stop the flames.

The authorities have reported dozens of wildfires in France, but the biggest and most worrying blazes are near the Atlantic coastline, in the southwestern region that includes Bordeaux.

One started on Wednesday in the Gironde area, while the other started on Thursday in the Landes area, farther south, according to local authorities. Those fires have burned over 120,000 acres so far.

The French authorities have also expressed concern about fires in the country’s southeastern Var area that have burned over 8,000 acres.

The fire in the Gironde area “generates its own winds, accelerates its spread and can abruptly change direction,” Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of France said late Friday.

“Civil protection experts had never before encountered such a phenomenon,” Mr. Lecornu said on social media after a government crisis meeting.

In Spain, wildfires in the mountains west of Madrid forced more than 19,000 people to evacuate and burned almost 15,000 acres by Friday afternoon. The blazes were closing in on populated areas.

“This is the worst wildfire in the Madrid region’s history,” Isabel Díaz Ayuso, the regional president, said on Friday. The fires spread amid “a perfect storm of extremely high temperatures and relentless winds,” she added, although the authorities in the Madrid region said on social media on Saturday that conditions had improved, with less wind, higher humidity and lower temperatures.

The Spanish and French authorities have ordered thousands to evacuate, set up emergency shelters, deployed firefighting planes and helicopters and sent security and military reinforcements to bolster hundreds of firefighters who are battling flames around the clock.

On Saturday, the prefect for the Gironde area ordered the evacuation of several western suburbs of Bordeaux as a precautionary measure. One includes the city’s airport. Thousands of people had previously evacuated the Cap Ferret peninsula, a popular Atlantic holiday destination. Hundreds fled by boat.

President Emmanuel Macron of France has asked the country’s armed forces “to mobilize to provide maximum support to civil security,” his office said on Friday evening. Over 1,000 soldiers are expected on the ground on Saturday, according to Mr. Lecornu, the prime minister.

The French authorities also announced on Friday that they were sending 1.5 million face masks to protect residents and emergency workers from toxic smoke caused by the fires.

The exact origins of the blazes in France and Spain were not immediately clear, but they are part of a broader surge of wildfires this summer across Europe fueled by repeated heat waves since late May.

The heat waves have parched vegetation and melted glaciers and have been linked to thousands of excess deaths. Last month was the hottest June on record in Western Europe, according to Copernicus, a European Union monitoring agency.

Connecting a specific heat wave or fire to global warming is hard to do, but experts agree that human-caused climate change is behind the increasingly high temperatures that have made wildfires more destructive in general.

About two weeks ago, a wildfire in the southeastern Spanish province of Almería killed 13 people, making it one of the country’s deadliest fires on record. Two French firefighters died battling a previous fire near Bordeaux this week.

France has decades of experience with wildfires in the country’s south, but the blazes have increased in number and pushed north as summer temperatures rise. By mid-July, almost 11,000 fires had already started across the country and burned more acres than throughout the entirety of last summer.

Carlos Barragán contributed reporting from Madrid.

item.title: From Defending Colombian Drug Traffickers to Waging War on Them
item.description:
In Miami, Abelardo De La Espriella moved in the murky world of “white powder” lawyers — high-priced defense lawyers who help accused Latin American drug traffickers and others avoid harsh sentences by turning them into U.S. government informants or witnesses.

He employed a former trafficker from Colombia who, court records show, helped South Florida lawyers find such business.

Mr. De La Espriella, a lawyer licensed in Colombia, often traveled to his homeland to meet clients embroiled in U.S. cases, including Alex Saab, a wealthy businessman indicted on charges of laundering millions on behalf of Venezuela’s leaders.

And he himself was scrutinized by federal prosecutors as they investigated Mr. Saab’s money laundering, according to five people with knowledge of the investigation into Mr. Saab.

Now, Mr. De La Espriella, with no past political experience, is suddenly Colombia’s next president, and promising to help the Trump administration escalate a regional drug war against the traffickers he once represented.

He returned to Colombia last year, reinventing himself as a law-and-order candidate determined to oust the left and wield an iron fist against the country’s criminals and resurgent armed trafficking groups. After receiving President Trump’s endorsement, he was elected in June.

Though his lavish Miami lifestyle of luxury cars, private jets and Italian designer suits may have been bankrolled in part by clients entangled in trafficking and laundering cases, he has pledged to help Mr. Trump crush “narcoterrorists,” bomb alleged drug boats and extradite accused traffickers.

In response to detailed questions about Mr. De La Espriella’s activities in Miami, his presidential office said in a statement that the matters “were extensively discussed during the presidential campaign” and that it did not “consider it appropriate to revisit them.”

But as Mr. De La Espriella prepares to take office in August, the opposition leader whom he defeated in the election, Iván Cepeda, is demanding answers about his work and relationships in the United States, urging supporters to mount a “peaceful resistance” until they are provided.

And with his best-known client, Mr. Saab, in U.S. custody awaiting trial on charges of acting as a financial agent for Venezuela’s former leader, Nicolás Maduro, more questions about Mr. De La Espriella’s past could emerge.

Mr. De La Espriella was himself scrutinized by federal prosecutors in Florida and New York as they investigated how Mr. Saab’s illicit funds moved through the U.S. financial system, according to the five people who spoke to The Times. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive political matter.

The precise focus of that scrutiny is not clear. But Mr. De La Espriella’s onetime employee, the former trafficker, pleaded guilty to laundering money from Mr. Saab’s overseas accounts around 2017. That money, court documents show, was intended to pay Mr. Saab’s lawyers, whose names were redacted from the documents, which do not provide any indication that the lawyers were part of the scheme.

Mr. De La Espriella was never charged. His office declined to respond to questions related to Mr. Saab. In its statement, it said, “The president was never investigated or charged in any of the matters you mention,” adding, “His conduct as a lawyer and as a private citizen has been absolutely impeccable.”

Republican lawmakers, including Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, have said he was vetted by U.S. officials. Representative María Elvira Salazar of Florida said on Colombia’s Election Day, “Abelardo De La Espriella doesn’t have any kind of investigation open in the United States.”

The Justice Department declined to comment.

When Mr. De La Espriella moved to Miami around 2013, he was seeking safety and a break from the heavy security detail that his risky work in Colombia had required, according to friends and political allies.

But there were also lucrative opportunities. Mr. De La Espriella, who is not licensed to practice law in Florida, opened a Miami office, brought on locally licensed lawyers and began spending time with the former trafficker, Jorge Luis Hernández.

Mr. Hernández was a known client hunter, and court documents say he worked as a paralegal with multiple South Florida law firms. He also worked for Mr. De La Espriella, according to three of the people who spoke to The Times. A Florida lawyer, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retribution, said Mr. Hernández described himself as Mr. De La Espriella’s assistant.

While Mr. Hernández was deeply involved in the so-called narco-defense world, court documents show he was also a longtime informant for federal law enforcement agencies, including the Drug Enforcement Administration. According to those filings, he had admitted to running drug shipments in fast boats from Colombia for right-wing paramilitary commanders before becoming an informant decades ago.

Colombia’s paramilitary forces rose to fight left-wing guerrillas, but became a scourge of their own, trafficking cocaine and committing atrocities. Early in his career, Mr. De La Espriella advocated for paramilitaries to be treated as political actors and defended politicians accused of having ties to the groups.

Mr. De La Espriella has acknowledged that he knew Mr. Hernández but has not publicly said they worked together.

During the campaign, their relationship sparked debate. Photos emerged of the two together, and critics called Mr. De La Espriella a “lawyer to the mafia,” a label he disputed. Mr. Cepeda questioned his suitability for office after the election, saying, “Abelardo De La Espriella has maintained a close connection with the paramilitary Jorge Luis Hernández.”

Mr. De La Espriella has said Mr. Saab came to him in 2013 seeking help with “reputational matters.” Venezuelan and Colombian journalists had raised questions about how Mr. Saab, a relatively obscure Colombian businessman, had obtained a Venezuelan government contract worth more than $150 million to supply materials for a housing program.

The two would seem an odd pair. While Mr. Saab worked with Venezuelan officials, Mr. De La Espriella was so opposed to Mr. Maduro, Venezuela’s former authoritarian president, that he wrote a book in 2018 making the case for his assassination.

Mr. De La Espriella has said that when U.S. authorities began investigating Mr. Saab, he urged him to cooperate and arranged meetings with federal agents. Mr. Saab ultimately refused, and his family fled to Venezuela in 2018 after Colombian officials said Mr. Saab was tipped off about a plan by Colombian authorities to arrest him.

Mr. De La Espriella has said he cut ties to Mr. Saab in 2019, after U.S. authorities indicted Mr. Saab and placed sanctions on him — as a U.S. permanent resident, he could not legally represent someone facing sanctions without a license.

In 2020, Mr. Saab was detained in Cape Verde. Before being extradited to the United States in 2021, he told Colombian journalists in an interview that Mr. De La Espriella no longer represented him, but had been “a great lawyer and friend.”

Around that time, Mr. De La Espriella’s Washington-based lawyer met with U.S. authorities to address his client’s exposure in the Saab investigation, according to two of the people who spoke to The Times.

According to these people, Mr. De La Espriella was investigated not for being Mr. Saab’s lawyer but in connection to the movement of Mr. Saab’s funds.

Prosecutors had charged Mr. Hernández with laundering more than $2.5 million from Mr. Saab’s overseas accounts into U.S. accounts alongside a former University of Miami professor, Bruce Bagley, who was charged in 2019.

According to the court documents that redact the lawyers’ names, the transfers took place between 2017 and 2018 and were meant to pay Mr. Saab’s lawyers in the United States for advising Mr. Saab and “accompanying him to meetings with the United States government” where Mr. Saab supplied information on the Maduro government.

Mr. Hernández and Mr. Bagley pleaded guilty to money laundering in the Southern District of New York. Mr. Hernández is now in U.S. custody on unrelated fraud charges. Lawyers for Mr. Hernández and Mr. Bagley declined to comment.

Among Mr. De La Espriella’s Miami acquaintances was a veteran D.E.A. agent who had overseen the investigation into Mr. Saab, according to two of the people who spoke to The Times. That agent was later indicted in an unrelated bribery scheme.

Mr. De La Espriella has declined to say how much Mr. Saab paid him, but Mr. De La Espriella’s longtime accountant, Daniel Diaz de la Rocha, said the lawyer had not grown fabulously wealthy because of his client. “Not by a stretch of the imagination,” he said in an interview.

Despite starting several businesses and showing off an extravagant lifestyle online — a private jet, jaunts to Italy, his own rum brand — Mr. De La Espriella was not extremely rich, Mr. Díaz said. His private jet was shared with others, Mr. Diaz said. He took out mortgages on his Miami homes, he said, which would not have been necessary if he had large sums on hand.

Mr. De La Espriella moved from a condo in a waterfront tower, to a house in Coral Gables, a well-heeled Miami suburb, and finally to a 7,500-square-foot mansion in Pinecrest that is now valued at more than $5 million. He also bought real estate in Colombia, records show.

The accountant, who was reached by phone and said he had not been asked by Mr. De La Espriella to speak to reporters, stressed that his businesses were legitimate. Mr. De La Espriella was a “straight shooter” in business, Mr. Díaz said, even if his ventures largely failed.

His recent businesses in Coral Gables — a piano bar, liquor store and gelato shop — all closed or were sold, Mr. Díaz noted.

“He’s more of an artist than a business person,” he said of Mr. De La Espriella, an amateur opera singer.

While running for president, Mr. De La Espriella often alluded to a fortune that allowed him to finance his campaign. But, Mr. Diaz said, except for his law firm in Colombia, “he lost in pretty much everything but real estate.”

This year, Mr. De La Espriella said he had stopped practicing law three years ago. Colombians who followed his career in Miami said he had become more of an influencer.

He promoted his fashion line, De La Espriella Style, started a podcast featuring Colombian luminaries, published noir fiction and worked out with the Miami-based trainer for Colombian reggaeton stars J Balvin and Maluma.

He opened the piano bar and restaurant Místico in Coral Gables in 2023 with partners including another Colombian music celebrity, Silvestre Dangond, with whom he launched the rum, Ron Defensor.

Mr. De La Espriella often took the microphone at Místico, belting out Italian classics like “O Sole Mio,” said Carlos Reyes Lesmes, the head bartender, and turned up at Místico and at his liquor store, Liquor Dreams, with former Colombian presidents.

At Liquor Dreams, which has been sold to new owners, Mr. De La Espriella often held court with a cigar and a drink in hand.

“This filled up because people wanted to come see him,” said María Sánchez, a liquor store employee from Colombia who said she had known Mr. De La Espriella since he was a boy.

After Mr. De La Espriella was naturalized as a U.S. citizen in 2023, he said he had found peace. But the following year, he packed up his family and left for Florence, saying only that he wanted his four children to connect with their Italian heritage.

Friends and associates say Mr. De La Espriella, who was a vocal critic of Colombia’s left-wing government, had been planning his presidential run before leaving Miami.

He reappeared in Colombia last year. Over the course of the campaign, he shed his old image as a sharply dressed lawyer, becoming a populist in a straw hat and soccer jersey.

Interviewers often asked him why he had traded his seeming picture-perfect life abroad for the dangers of Colombian politics. His response was that God — and patriotic duty — had called.

He had to save Colombia from drug traffickers.

Jorge Valencia contributed reporting from Bogotá, Colombia, and Genevieve Glatsky contributed reporting from Barranquilla, Colombia. Alain Delaquérière contributed research.

]]>

item.title: India’s Education Minister Steps Down, Handing Win to Protesters
item.description:
India’s education minister stepped down on Saturday, in a major victory for a student protest movement whose explosive rise has become one of the most serious challenges in years to the power of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, submitted his resignation to Mr. Modi, bowing to weeks of public pressure that culminated in nationwide street protests from Delhi and Mumbai to Kolkata and Chennai.

Mr. Pradhan said he had been “deeply pained” by the events of recent days, but he pointed a finger at what he called “anti-national forces,” saying he did not want them to take advantage of the massive protests.

The movement emerged in May, powered by widespread anger and frustration after the government ordered millions of students to retake an extremely competitive national medical school entrance exam because test questions had been leaked. Students held Mr. Pradhan, under whose watch several national exams were marred by leaks, responsible.

Loud cheers erupted at the protest site near Jantar Mantar, an 18th century observatory in New Delhi, as protesters heard the news that Mr. Pradhan had resigned.

“This is democracy,” said Abhijeet Dipke, the 30-year-old founder of a youth movement that in two months has jolted Indian politics. But it wasn’t immediately clear that the protesters would call it a day. In a statement, Mr. Dipke said protesters had made more demands of the government. “We won’t go like this.”

Mr. Dipke founded a satirical party called the Cockroach Janta Party in May after a disparaging remark by India’s top judge comparing India’s youth to cockroaches. The party quickly became the vehicle through which millions of young Indians began to express their frustrations about a troubled education system and a lack of job opportunities.

The C.J.P. was founded just days after the medical school exam was canceled. Mr. Pradhan’s education ministry announced a fresh date for the test, but in the interim, at least 21 students died by suicide, according to the C.J.P.’s count.

Mr. Dipke’s C.J.P. began protesting in June, but the movement gained momentum this month, after the police cracked down with force on demonstrators as thousands marched to Parliament in New Delhi on Monday. Protests had spread to major cities across India.

One of the demands Mr. Dipke and other leaders of the movement put before the government was compensation of 10 million rupees (about $103,000) for the families of the children who took their own lives.

Mr. Dipke said his group also wanted accountability for security forces who cracked down on Monday’s peaceful protesters. “Action must be taken against the police officers for that,” he said.

Mr. Pradhan was previously largely dismissive of the protests. In a social media post he accused opposition parties of exploiting students to “manufacture disruption,” and in a June interview with a local media outlet referred to the student protesters as “the B-team of terrorists.” But that appeared only to strengthen the resolve of the students to remove him. Despite winning some rare concessions from the government, they vowed to continue the protests until the minister was dismissed.

The call to remove Mr. Pradhan forced Mr. Modi to balance loyalty to his supporters against the need to placate young people, who account for 40 percent of India’s population. An operative of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, Mr. Pradhan was credited with helping the B.J.P. come to power in some recent state elections. Over a nearly three-decade political career, he has held various positions in the party.

But the exam leak scandal in May triggered long-simmering frustrations about government accountability and a lack of jobs and opportunity that Mr. Modi cannot immediately address. India puts students through a pressure-cooker education system, and yet nearly 40 percent of graduates between the ages of 15 and 25 are unemployed, according to a 2026 study. Student suicides are increasing faster than those of the overall population.

The students’ victory could motivate them to push their demands further. Aside from education, the C.J.P. is also asking the government to consider its far more sweeping agenda for change, including judicial reforms and gender quotas for Parliament.
